lead: Theodolite work is how a surveyor measures angles to 20 seconds and turns them into heights, distances and a control frame for the whole site. After this unit you can adjust and read a theodolite, run trig levelling and tacheometry, plan a triangulation or trilateration network, combine repeated observations by weights, and set out horizontal and vertical curves.
about: This unit is about turning lines of sight into numbers you can trust. 4.1 takes the theodolite apart and shows the geometry its adjustments restore; 4.2 uses it to read horizontal and vertical angles; 4.3 turns a vertical angle and a measured distance into a height. 4.4 gets distance and elevation from a single sighting, 4.5 builds a triangulation or trilateration frame, and 4.6 places that frame as horizontal and vertical control under the whole survey. 4.7 combines repeated and unequal observations by weights and least squares, and 4.8 applies the same angles to setting out circular, transition and vertical curves on the ground.

chapters.idea: A theodolite is a precision angle instrument held together by three mutually perpendicular axes, and its adjustments are nothing but the job of restoring that geometry.
chapters.depth: Parts and the job of each: telescope with focusing screw, diaphragm and cross hairs, vertical circle, horizontal circle read by two verniers A and B (20″ least count on a common vernier theodolite) or by an optical micrometer, upper and lower plates, inner and outer spindles, foot screws, plate levels, altitude (spil) level, clamps and tangent screws, optical plummet, tribrach. Temporary adjustment, done at every station: setting over the mark, levelling with the foot screws, focusing the eyepiece and objective until parallax goes. Permanent adjustment, done rarely and by a trained hand: plate level axis perpendicular to vertical axis; vertical hair in the plane of the line of collimation (diaphragm test); telescope level parallel to the line of collimation; line of collimation perpendicular to the horizontal axis (collimation test); horizontal axis perpendicular to vertical axis (spindle test); vertical circle index set with the altitude bubble. Give the field test and the correction for each. Define face left, face right and transiting. Some syllabi say 'transit theodolite' for the same instrument.

chapters.example: A 20″ vernier theodolite is levelled on a station and the plate level bubble is brought to the centre of its run. The telescope is transited through 180° and the bubble now stands 4 divisions off centre. One division of the bubble tube is 30″. Find the error between the plate level axis and the vertical axis, and the correction. Answer: the bubble shows twice the axis error, so the error is 4/2 = 2 divisions = 60″. Bring the bubble back by 2 divisions with the plate level capstan screws, re-level with the foot screws, and repeat until it stays centred through 180°.
chapters.trap: Treating the whole bubble drift as the axis error and correcting 4 divisions when only 2 are wrong. The second trap is mixing temporary adjustments, made at every setup, with permanent adjustments, made once and only when a test fails.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: measurement of lengths and angles, least count of a vernier.
chapters.leave: Bearings, meridians and traverse booking to Unit 2; levelling instruments and their own adjustments to Unit 3; the electronic theodolite inside a total station to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A horizontal angle is the difference between two directions taken with the lower plate clamped and released in turn, and a vertical angle is a vertical-circle reading corrected for its quadrant and for the face.
chapters.depth: Horizontal angles: ordinary method on both faces; repetition method (the angle is turned n times and the total read divided by n, which blunts graduation error); reiteration or direction method for several directions from one station, with the horizon closed and the closing error shared out equally. Vernier reading: degrees from the main scale, minutes and seconds from the vernier whose zero lies inside the interval, quoted as a mean of vernier A and vernier B after taking 180° off B. Vertical angles: how the vertical circle is graduated (from the horizontal, or from the zenith — say which), elevation and depression, the rule that connects a zenith reading to an altitude, and the mean of face left and face right. Errors in theodolite work: eccentricity of centres, collimation, vertical axis not truly vertical, graduation error, bisection and refraction. Keep the traverse booking and closing error to Unit 2.

figure.title: Angle on both faces
figure.aria: Five boxes in a row from setting up the instrument to taking the mean of the face left and face right readings of one horizontal angle.

chapters.example: A horizontal angle AOB is measured by the repetition method with a 20″ theodolite, starting from a zero reading. After 4 repetitions the vernier reads 148°24′40″, so angle AOB = 148°24′40″ / 4 = 37°06′10″. Check with the two faces: face left gave 37°06′20″ and face right gave 37°06′00″. Their mean is 37°06′10″, and the half difference of 10″ is the collimation error.
chapters.trap: Reading face right at face value: vernier A stands about 180° away, so B is reduced and A is not. A vertical angle taken from the wrong quadrant, or a depression angle entered as positive, wrecks the next chapter.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for the axes, clamps, tangent screws and the meaning of face left and face right.
chapters.leave: Traverse angles, latitudes and departures to Unit 2; curvature and refraction corrections to angles over long lines get only a mention here and belong to Unit 3 for levelling.

chapters.idea: A vertical angle plus a horizontal distance gives a height, so an object that cannot be touched can still be levelled.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Object with an accessible base: height above the instrument axis = D tan α, then add the instrument height and subtract the target height. Object with an inaccessible base, both stations in the same vertical plane as the object (single plane method): with instrument axes at the same level or at different levels, the horizontal distance comes from D = s tan α₂ / (tan α₁ − tan α₂), where s is the distance between stations. Stations not in the same vertical plane as the object (double plane method): horizontal angles and the base give the two horizontal distances, then two heights are computed and averaged. Angle of elevation and angle of depression and the sign each carries. Curvature and refraction: state that the combined correction is about 0.0673 D² m with D in km and that it is derived in Unit 3; do not re-derive it. Uses: height of a gopuram, a bridge pier, a chimney, a hill top, a tower whose base is inside a compound.

figure.aria: Decision tree of trigonometric levelling cases: base accessible, or base inaccessible split into single plane with equal or unequal axis levels, and double plane.

chapters.example: Two instrument stations P and Q are 60.000 m apart, in the same vertical plane as the top of a tower, with Q farther away. The vertical angles to the top are 12°30′ from P and 9°18′ from Q. The instrument height is 1.45 m at both stations, and the target is the top itself. Find the horizontal distance from P and the height of the top above the ground at P. tan 12°30′ = 0.22169 and tan 9°18′ = 0.16376, difference = 0.05793. D = 60 × 0.16376 / 0.05793 = 169.6 m. Height above the instrument axis = 169.6 × 0.22169 = 37.60 m. Height above ground = 37.60 + 1.45 = 39.05 m.
chapters.trap: Putting a slant distance into D tan α, and forgetting that the answer is a height above the instrument axis, so the instrument height must still be added and the target height subtracted. Depression angles need the opposite sign.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.1 and 4.2 for setting up and reading a vertical angle on both faces; Unit 3 for curvature, refraction and reduced levels.
chapters.leave: Curvature and refraction in full, and all levelling book keeping, to Unit 3; tacheometric ways of getting the distance to Unit 4.4.

chapters.idea: A length held at the far station subtends a measurable angle, and that angle gives both the horizontal distance and the elevation in one sighting, with no chaining.
chapters.depth: Principle of tacheometry: distance from the angle subtended by a known length. Stadia system with fixed hairs and with movable hairs; the anallatic lens and why it makes C zero. Tacheometric constants K = f/i and C = f + d, usually K = 100 and C between 0 and 0.3 m. Horizontal line of sight: D = K s + C, where s is the staff intercept. Inclined line of sight with the staff held vertical: D = K s cos²θ + C cosθ and V = K s sinθ cosθ + C sinθ, where θ is the vertical angle. Staff normal to the line of sight gets one line only. Subtense method: a fixed base of 2 m on a subtense bar, D = s / (2 tan(θ/2)) ≈ s/θ for small θ in radians; also the two-instrument version with the base at the instrument. Tangential method with two vertical angles to two targets: D = s / (tan α₁ − tan α₂), used when staff readings are unreliable. Uses: contouring, filling detail fast across a river or a crowded street. Total-station tacheometry in one line only.

chapters.example: A tacheometer with K = 100 and C = 0 sights a staff held vertically. The intercept between the top and bottom hairs is 1.250 m and the vertical angle is 8°12′. The mid hair reads 1.850 m and the reduced level of the instrument axis is 102.500 m. Find D, V and the reduced level of the staff station. cos 8°12′ = 0.98978 and sin 8°12′ = 0.14263. D = 100 × 1.250 × 0.98978² = 125 × 0.97966 = 122.46 m. V = 125 × 0.14263 × 0.98978 = 17.65 m. RL = 102.500 + 17.65 − 1.850 = 118.300 m.
chapters.trap: Using D = 100 s on an inclined sight and dropping the cos²θ factor. In the subtense method the angle must be in radians for D = s/θ, and θ there is the whole angle subtended by the bar, not half of it.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for vertical angles, chapter 4.1 for the instrument; Unit 3 for reduced levels; Unit 1 for the idea of a subtended angle and EDM.
chapters.leave: Total-station and EDM hardware details to Unit 5; contour drawing and interpolation to Unit 3; the least-squares treatment of tacheometric error to chapter 4.7.

chapters.idea: A control frame is a chain of triangles in which one side is measured with great care and the rest are computed from well-shaped observed angles, or every side is measured directly by trilateration.
chapters.depth: Triangulation principle: measure a base line precisely, observe the angles to 20″, get the other sides by the sine rule and carry coordinates forward. Classification into primary, secondary and tertiary (first, second and third order) control. Layout: base net, main chain of triangles, subsidiary triangles, satellite or eccentric stations with reduction to centre in outline. Well-conditioned triangle: no angle below 30° or above 120°, best near 60°, because the sine changes slowly there; strength of figure as a way of comparing layouts. Field work: reconnaissance, station marking, signals with their height and the effect of refraction, towers and scaffolds. Base measurement by tape or EDM with corrections and reduction to mean sea level in one line. Trilateration: all three sides measured by EDM and the angles found by the cosine rule; what each method needs on the ground and which is easier today. Coordinate computation from a base and its azimuth.

figure.aria: A chain of three triangles A-B-D, B-D-E and B-E-C standing on the measured base AB, with BC as a check base.

chapters.example: In triangle ABC the base AB = 500.000 m is measured. The observed angles are A = 62°18′ and B = 57°42′, so C = 180° − 120°00′ = 60°00′. Find the sides BC and AC. sin 62°18′ = 0.88539 and sin 57°42′ = 0.84526, sin 60°00′ = 0.86603. BC = AB sin A / sin C = 500 × 0.88539 / 0.86603 = 511.18 m. AC = AB sin B / sin C = 500 × 0.84526 / 0.86603 = 488.02 m. The two computed sides add to 999.20 m, well above the base of 500.000 m, so the triangle is sound.
chapters.trap: Pairing a side with the wrong angle in the sine rule, and calling a thin triangle a strong one. Strength comes from angles near 60°; a very acute angle makes the computed side very sensitive to angle error.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.1 and 4.2 for angles on both faces; Unit 2 for azimuths, coordinates and the idea of a closing error.
chapters.leave: Traverse computations and closing error correction to Unit 2; EDM and GNSS as distance and control tools to Unit 5; the least-squares adjustment of a triangulation net to chapter 4.7.

chapters.idea: Control is a sparse set of points of higher accuracy than the detail survey itself, fixed first by horizontal and vertical methods, and every later measurement is hung on it.
chapters.depth: Definition, purpose and why control comes before detail. Horizontal control by triangulation, trilateration, traversing and GNSS; vertical control by precise differential levelling and by trigonometric levelling where the ground is too rough. Order and density: national first-order networks down to third order, then minor control for the detail survey; the order fixes the permitted relative misclosure, and tighter order means smaller. Benchmarks, permanent marks and their descriptions as a record for later work. Ground control points for photogrammetry, UAV flights and for GIS base mapping. Checks that prove a control network: closing the horizon, closing on a known point, comparing a measured check base, loop closure in levelling. Setting out of structures, road alignments and pipelines hangs on the same control.

figure.aria: Tree splitting control into horizontal control by triangulation, traverse and GNSS, and vertical control by differential and trigonometric levelling.

chapters.example: A level run starts at benchmark A with RL 250.000 m, goes 6 km round a loop and closes back on A. The field book gives ΣBS = 12.824 m and ΣFS = 12.798 m. Find the misclosure and decide whether to accept the run if the permissible misclosure is 12√K mm, with K in km. ΣBS − ΣFS = +0.026 m = +26 mm, and for a loop that returns to the same mark this is the misclosure. Permissible = 12√6 = 29.4 mm. Since 26 mm is under 29.4 mm, the run is accepted and the 26 mm is distributed over the setups, or in proportion to distance, with the opposite sign.
chapters.trap: Confusing control with the detail survey. Control is observed first, to a tighter standard, and detail is hung on it. A closing error inside the permitted limit is distributed, not ignored, and a run outside it is repeated.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.2 and 4.5 for angles and the horizontal frame; Unit 3 for differential levelling and booking; chapter 4.3 for trig levelling.
chapters.leave: Booking and reduction methods, curvature and refraction, and contouring to Unit 3; GNSS positioning modes and satellite geometry to Unit 5; map projections and coordinates in GIS to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Observations of unequal quality are combined by weights that fall as the error variance rises, and the most probable values are the ones that make the weighted sum of squared residuals a minimum.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. True value, observed value, error, residual. Weight w = k/σ²: the weight of the mean of n observations is n times that of one; the weight of a levelled difference falls as 1/L for a run of length L; the weight of a taped distance falls as 1/L; the weight of an angle rises with the number of repetitions. Laws of weights for sums, differences and products in outline. Principle of least squares: choose the unknowns so that Σ w v² is least. Normal equations for direct observations of one quantity, which reduce to the weighted mean, and the two-unknown setup for indirect observations in symbols only. Probable error, standard error of a single observation and of the weighted mean, and the 3σ rule for a doubtful reading. One worked network adjustment, a level loop or a braced quadrilateral, as a demonstration.

figure.title: Weighted adjustment
figure.aria: Flowchart of a weighted least-squares adjustment, from observations and weights to the normal equations, the solution, the residuals and a re-check for outliers.

chapters.example: The difference of level between two points is measured by three levelling runs: h₁ = 12.436 m over 2 km, h₂ = 12.448 m over 3 km and h₃ = 12.440 m over 5 km. Find the most probable difference of level. Weights are proportional to 1/L, so take 1/2, 1/3 and 1/5, which scale to 15, 10 and 6, sum 31. Weighted mean = (15 × 12.436 + 10 × 12.448 + 6 × 12.440) / 31 = 385.660 / 31 = 12.441 m. The residuals are −0.005 m, +0.007 m and −0.001 m, so Σ w v² is small and none of the runs is rejected.
chapters.trap: Making the weight proportional to the length of the run. It is the reverse: w ∝ 1/L, because a long run accumulates error as √L and must pull the mean less. Also, weights carry the squared error, not the error.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for repeated angle observations and chapter 4.6 for control runs; Unit 1 for systematic and random error, accuracy and precision.
chapters.leave: Error propagation and the statistics of measurement to Unit 1; traverse adjustment by Bowditch and transit rules to Unit 2; adjustment of large GNSS networks to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Geometry and chainage are joined by a curve, and every point on it can be set out from the tangent by an offset or a deflection angle computed from the radius.
chapters.depth: Simple circular curve: T = R tan(Δ/2), L = πRΔ/180, long chord = 2R sin(Δ/2), E = R(sec(Δ/2) − 1), M = R(1 − cos(Δ/2)), chainage of the tangent points from the intersection point. Degree of curve by the arc definition, as used for Indian roads. Setting out by offsets from the long chord, offsets from the tangent, Rankine's deflection angles, and by total station in one line only. Transition curve: why the curvature cannot jump from zero to 1/R, so centrifugal force and superelevation need a ramp; clothoid (spiral, used as a cubic parabola for small angles) and lemniscate; length L = V³/(C R) with V in m/s and C the rate of change of radial acceleration, and the cant formula as an alternative; shift and the tangent length of a curve with transitions. Vertical curve: summit and valley, parabolic, length by rate of change of grade and by sight distance, RL on the curve from the tangent RL plus the tangent correction.

figure.aria: Two curves from the same tangent point: the circular offset climbs as x squared to about 8.3 m at 50 m, while the cubic transition climbs to only about 2.8 m.

chapters.example: A circular curve of radius R = 300 m deflects an alignment by Δ = 40°, and the intersection point is at chainage 2450.000 m. Find the elements and the chainages of the tangent points, and the transition length for a design speed of 80 km/h with C = 0.3 m/s³. T = 300 tan 20° = 109.19 m; L = π × 300 × 40 / 180 = 209.44 m; long chord = 2 × 300 × sin 20° = 205.21 m; E = 300(sec 20° − 1) = 19.25 m; M = 300(1 − cos 20°) = 18.09 m. T₁ = 2450.000 − 109.19 = 2340.81 m and T₂ = 2450.000 + 109.19 = 2559.19 m. Speed 80 km/h = 22.22 m/s, so transition length = 22.22³ / (0.3 × 300) = 10973 / 90 = 121.9 m.
chapters.trap: Using the full deflection angle Δ where Δ/2 belongs in T = R tan(Δ/2), and mixing the degree of curve with metres of radius. A sharper curve, a smaller radius, needs a longer transition, not a shorter one.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.2 for deflection angles and 4.4 for fast setting out of detail; Unit 1 for chainage, offsets and scales; Unit 2 for setting out by coordinates.
chapters.leave: Superelevation limits, sight distance and the design of the road itself to highway engineering; setting out of the whole alignment by coordinates to Unit 5.
